stem: If point T divides the segment AB with A(\(-7\), 4) and B(\(-6\), \(-5\)) in the ratio 7 : 2, find the co-ordinates of T.
solution:
Let the co-ordinates of T be \((x, y)\).

\(\therefore\) by the section formula,

\(x = \dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n} = \dfrac{7 \times (-6) + 2 \times (-7)}{7 + 2} = \dfrac{-42 - 14}{9} = \dfrac{-56}{9}\)

\(y = \dfrac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n} = \dfrac{7 \times (-5) + 2 \times (4)}{7 + 2} = \dfrac{-35 + 8}{9} = \dfrac{-27}{9} = -3\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of point T are \(\left(\dfrac{-56}{9}, -3\right)\).

stem: If point P(\(-4\), 6) divides the line segment AB with A(\(-6\), 10) and B(r, s) in the ratio 2 : 1, find the co-ordinates of B.
solution:
By section formula

\(-4 = \dfrac{2 \times r + 1 \times (-6)}{2 + 1}\)

\(\therefore -4 = \dfrac{2r - 6}{3}\)

\(\therefore -12 = 2r - 6\)

\(\therefore 2r = -6\)

\(\therefore r = -3\)

\(6 = \dfrac{2 \times s + 1 \times 10}{2 + 1}\)

\(\therefore 6 = \dfrac{2s + 10}{3}\)

\(\therefore 18 = 2s + 10\)

\(\therefore 2s = 8\)

\(\therefore s = 4\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of point B are \((-3, 4)\).

stem: A(15, 5), B(9, 20) and A\(-\)P\(-\)B. Find the ratio in which point P(11, 15) divides segment AB.
solution:
Suppose, point P(11, 15) divides segment AB in the ratio \(m : n\)

\(\therefore\) by section formula,

\(x = \dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}\)

\(\therefore 11 = \dfrac{9m + 15n}{m + n}\)

\(\therefore 11m + 11n = 9m + 15n\)

\(\therefore 2m = 4n\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{4}{2} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)

\(\therefore\) The required ratio is 2 : 1.

(The book adds beside this working: "Similarly, find the ratio using \(y\) co-ordinates. Write the conclusion." Doing so gives \(15 = \dfrac{20m + 5n}{m + n}\), so \(15m + 15n = 20m + 5n\), \(10n = 5m\), \(\dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{2}{1}\) — the same ratio 2 : 1.)

stem: Find the co-ordinates of the points of trisection of the segment joining the points A(2, \(-2\)) and B(\(-7\), 4). (The two points that divide the line segment in three equal parts are called as points of trisection of the segment.)
solution:
[Textbook note: while dealing with point Q the book prints "\(\dfrac{AQ}{QD} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)"; there is no point D in this figure and the ratio meant is \(\dfrac{AQ}{QB} = \dfrac{2}{1}\). The working and the answers are unaffected.]

Let points P and Q be the points of trisection of the line segment joining the points A and B.

Point P and Q divide line segment AB into three parts.

AP = PQ = QB  .......... (I)

\(\dfrac{AP}{PB} = \dfrac{AP}{PQ + QB} = \dfrac{AP}{AP + AP} = \dfrac{AP}{2AP} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  .......... From (I)

Point P divides seg AB in the ratio 1 : 2.

\(x\) co-ordinate of point P \(= \dfrac{1 \times (-7) + 2 \times 2}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{-7 + 4}{3} = \dfrac{-3}{3} = -1\)

\(y\) co-ordinate of point P \(= \dfrac{1 \times 4 + 2 \times (-2)}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{4 - 4}{3} = \dfrac{0}{3} = 0\)

Point Q divides seg AB in the ratio 2 : 1.  \(\therefore \dfrac{AQ}{QB} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)

\(x\) co-ordinate of point Q \(= \dfrac{2 \times (-7) + 1 \times 2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{-14 + 2}{3} = \dfrac{-12}{3} = -4\)

\(y\) co-ordinate of point Q \(= \dfrac{2 \times 4 + 1 \times -2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{8 - 2}{3} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of points of trisection are \((-1, 0)\) and \((-4, 2)\).
note: The book prints "AQ/QD = 2/1" where it means AQ/QB — there is no point D in Fig. 5.18. Recorded as an errata bracket; the derivation and both answers are correct.
